titles.225: Annotatio III §.VI open: Two famous post-Reformation Consociation attempts — LIPSIACUM (1631) and CASSELLANUM (1661); the prior distinguished three ways
titles.226: Annotatio III §.VI (1): Reformed at Leipzig ready to subscribe the Invariata — Variata not rejected; Nauenburg 1561 precedent; Brandenburg/Hessian Relation confession
titles.227: Annotatio III §.VI (2): Colloquy end — both sides measure Augsburg-article agreement and hope closer union; mutual Christian love stipulated
titles.228: Annotatio III §.VI (3): Frankfurt Estates (third year after) approve the Leipzig Colloquy and decree Saxony and Brandenburg continue the Protestant peace work

latin.225:
§. VI.
Seculi Reformationem insecuti, Duo famosissima, Protestantes inter se conciliandi, numerantur Molimina, LIPSIACUM unum, Theologis Saxonicis, Brandenburgicis & Hassiaciis An. 1631; alterum CASSELLANUM, ab Hassiaciis solis, Marpurgensibus scilicet & Rintelenfibus, A. 1661, Collocutoribus, celebrata. PRIUS triplici nomine perquam insigne.
latin.226: (1) Quòd sub ipsum initium Reformati Theologi, Confessioni Augustanae Invariatae sese addicere nulli dubitarunt, paratissimi etiam subscribere eidem, quandocunque istud altera pars desideraret, non rejectâ interim aut repudiata Variata, seu Philippicâ, defensâ verò eô modô, quô Status Imperii in Conventu Nauenburgico An. 1561. hanc quoque ipsam admittendam duxerant. Cum hujus Reformatorum Lipsiensium facti jam aliquoties meminerimus, juvabit hôc locô verba eorum huc facientia in medium adducere, ex Relatione de Colloquio Lipsiaco, germanica.
latin.227: (2.) Quòd in fine Colloquii, utraque pars, eum in finem Colloquium inter se habitum innuit, quò innotesceret, tum quousque in Articulis Aug. Confess. consentirent, tum quae spes superesset, unionis arctioris in posterum ineundae, ad ampliandam veram Christi Ecclesiam & extinguendam Pontificiorum Fiduciam, ex Dissidio Protestantium istis subnatam, dum intereà Christianum amorem sibi invicem stipulati essent.
latin.228: Denique (3.) quòd Status Imperii, tertio post anno, Francofurti ad Moenum congregati, non tantum Colloqv. Lipf. aprobarunt, sed Spe Theologorum Lipsiensium se haud frustratum iri arbitrati, Decreto peculiari sanciverunt, Electores Serenissimos, Saxonicum & Brandenburgicum, publico suo nomine rogandos esse, quò Pacis Protestanticae Negotium, Lipsiae inchoatum, plurium Theologorum moderatiorum operâ, continuandum, & ad felicem exitum perducendum curarent. Decretum Statuum, cùm ad paucorum notitiam pervenerit, exhibemus hic Lectori nostro, iis verbis, quibus illud in Joh. Durai Prodromo Irenicorum descriptum legimus, pag. 1.
latin.229:
DECRETUM ORDINUM EVANGELICORUM Francofurti factum.
Posteaquam in praesenti Evangelicorum, qui ex Imperii Circulis adsunt, Ordinum & Eorum, qui absunt, Legatorum & Deputatorum conventu, Johannes Duraeus, Evangelicus Theologus, Unionis fraternaeque Reconciliationis inter Evangelicos, tàm intra, quàm extra Imperium Ecclesias in Capitibus Christiana Evangelicaque Religionis nostra fundamentalibus stabiliendae negotium, aliquoties antehac propositum & considerationi objectum, iterum proposuisset, & in spectabili Deputatorum consessu, ab omnibus confæderatis Statibus auditus fuisset, ac multorum utriusque partis tàm in Germania, quàm Gallia, Anglia & Transylvania, praestantissimorum Theologorum & Academiarum protulisset sententias de viis, quibus Christianus iste atque in se laudabilis unitatis scopus obtineatur; cumque unanimi planè consensu Sex Imperii praenominati Circuli prolatas praedictorum Theologorum sententias perpendentes, hoc equidem opus Domino Deo, ut pacis Deo, gratum, laudabile, summeque necessarium & Evangelicis Ecclesiis omni modo utile & commodum judicassent, simul tamen estimassent, illud esse magni ponderis atque momenti negotium, de quo multi Legatorum ac Deputatorum, qui hac vice aderant, nullas haberent Instructiones: Ideo praesentes Statuum Legati atque Deputati receperunt, se rem recto Instituto propositam, & sententias Theologorum unà communicatas, fideliter relaturos.
latin.230: Adhaec quaedam optimo animo a Legatis quibusdam proposita fuere: nempe, quòd ab una parte consultum judicabant, ut praedictam Declarationem (quae de modo procedendi, quem praenominatus Duraeus proposuit, deque via, pacificorum quorundam Theologorum colloquium, in quo unanimis fidei de fundamentalibus salutis nostrae capitibus confessio institui possit, ad exemplum amicae illius collationis, quae ante triennium Lipziae inter Theologos Electorales Saxonicos, Brandenburgicos & Hassiacos-Cassellanos inita fuit) primo quoque tempore superiores Imperii Circuli mittant; atque ut ab hisce Electoribus invitentur scriptis Literis Invitoriis tam exteri Principes & Reges: Ab alia autem parte Alii hanc quoque proponebant utilem rationem, ut salvis cujusque Electoris, Principis & Status praetensionibus & juribus, rogarentur Serenissimi Electores Saxonicus atque Brandenburgicus, dignentur inceptam Lipziae ante tres annos amicam collationem continuare, atque hunc in finem conventum indicere, cui etiam alii utriusque partis evocati pacifici Theologi intersint; atque in eo conventu buc praesertim fore respiciendum, ut consensus, quoad fieri potest, modestè ineatur in Christiana atque unanimi Confessione, quae contineat omnia & singula, quae salutis fundamentum concernunt, Religionis capita: in reliquis autem capitibus disputationem atque contentionem Scholasticam esse seponendam. Praeter haec etiam & in hoc aliqui amicam consensionem suam apertè declararunt; quòd intereà temporis omnis ab utraque parte tàm in docendo, quàm scribendo Christiana moderatio & lenitas usurpanda sit; atque hoc fine, in utriusque partis templis, publicas preces esse concipiendas, quibus negotium Deo O. M. commendetur. In cujus rei testimonium hic recessus hac de re factus est. Actum Francofurti ad Moenum 14. Sept. Anno 1634.

pass_a.225: §. VI. Following the Reformation century, two most famous Efforts of reconciling Protestants among themselves are counted, one the LEIPZIG one, by Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian Theologians in the year 1631; the other the CASSEL one, celebrated by Hessian collocutors alone, namely Marburg and Rinteln ones, in the year 1661. The PRIOR is exceedingly distinguished by a threefold title.
pass_a.226: (1) That under the very beginning the Reformed Theologians did not hesitate to addict themselves to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, being most ready also to subscribe the same whenever the other party should desire that, the Variata or Philippica meanwhile not rejected or repudiated, but defended in that manner in which the Estates of the Empire in the Nauenburg Convention in the year 1561 had judged that this same one also ought to be admitted. Since we have already remembered this deed of the Leipzig Reformers several times, it will help in this place to bring into the midst their words making for this, from the German Relation concerning the Leipzig Colloquy.
pass_a.227: (2.) That at the end of the Colloquy, either party intimates that the Colloquy held among themselves was to this end, that it might become known both how far they agreed in the Articles of the Augsburg Confession, and what hope remained of a closer union to be entered thereafter, for enlarging the true Church of Christ and extinguishing the confidence of the Pontiffs born from that Dissension of the Protestants, while meanwhile they had stipulated Christian love to one another.
pass_a.228: Finally (3.) that the Estates of the Empire, gathered at Frankfurt on the Main in the third year afterward, not only approved the Leipzig Colloquy, but judging that they would scarcely be frustrated of the Hope of the Leipzig Theologians, sanctioned by a peculiar Decree that the Most Serene Electors, the Saxon and the Brandenburg, were to be asked in their public name, that they should care that the Business of Protestant Peace, begun at Leipzig, be continued by the labor of several more moderate Theologians, and be led through to a happy outcome. The Decree of the Estates, since it has come to the knowledge of few, we exhibit here to our Reader, in those words in which we read it described in John Dury’s Prodromus of Irenic Works, page 1.
pass_a.229: DECREE OF THE EVANGELICAL ORDERS made at Frankfurt. Afterward, in the present convention of the Evangelical Orders who are present from the Circles of the Empire and of the Legates and Deputies of those who are absent, John Dury, Evangelical Theologian, had again proposed the business of establishing Union and fraternal Reconciliation among Evangelicals, churches both within and outside the Empire, in the fundamental Heads of our Christian and Evangelical Religion, a business proposed before and cast for consideration; and in a notable session of Deputies he had been heard by all the confederated Estates, and had brought forth the judgments of many most outstanding Theologians and Academies of either party in Germany as in France, England, and Transylvania concerning the ways by which that Christian and in itself praiseworthy aim of unity may be obtained; and when with plainly unanimous consent the Six aforementioned Circles of the Empire, weighing the judgments brought forth of the aforesaid Theologians, had judged this work indeed grateful to the Lord God as God of peace, praiseworthy, and most necessary and in every way useful and advantageous to Evangelical Churches, yet at the same time had estimated it to be a business of great weight and moment, concerning which many of the Legates and Deputies who were present this turn had no Instructions: Therefore the present Legates and Deputies of the Estates received that they would faithfully report the matter proposed by right Institute, and the judgments of the Theologians communicated together.
pass_a.230: Besides these things certain proposals were made in best spirit by certain Legates: namely, that on one side they judged it advisable that the aforesaid Declaration (which concerns the mode of proceeding which the aforenamed Dury proposed, and the way of a colloquy of certain peaceable Theologians in which a unanimous confession of faith concerning the fundamental heads of our salvation can be instituted, after the example of that friendly collation which three years before was begun at Leipzig among Electoral Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian-Cassel Theologians) the upper Circles of the Empire should send at the first opportunity; and that by these Electors both foreign Princes and Kings should be invited by written Letters of Invitation: But on the other side Others also proposed this useful plan, that with each Elector’s, Prince’s, and Estate’s pretensions and rights saved, the Most Serene Electors Saxon and Brandenburg should be asked to deign to continue the friendly collation begun at Leipzig three years before, and to that end to appoint a convention at which other peaceable Theologians of either party summoned should also be present; and that in that convention regard should especially be had that consensus, so far as can be done, be modestly entered in a Christian and unanimous Confession which contains each and every head of Religion that concerns the foundation of salvation: but in the remaining heads scholastic dispute and contention is to be set aside. Besides these things also some openly declared their friendly consent in this: that meanwhile all Christian moderation and mildness is to be used by either party both in teaching and in writing; and to this end public prayers are to be framed in the temples of either party, by which the business may be commended to God Most High. In testimony of which matter this recess concerning this thing was made. Done at Frankfurt on the Main, 14 September, year 1634.

225: §. VI. After the Reformation century come two most famous Consociation attempts at reconciling Protestants with one another.
One is the Leipzig attempt — Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian theologians, 1631; the other the Cassel attempt — Hessian collocutors alone (Marburg and Rinteln), 1661.
The prior (Leipzig) is marked out in three ways.
226: (1) Right at the start the Reformed theologians did not hesitate to bind themselves to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, and were fully ready to subscribe it whenever the other side asked — without rejecting or repudiating the Variata (Philippica), which they defended as the Imperial Estates had admitted it at the Nauenburg Convention in 1561.
Since this Leipzig Reformed act has been remembered before, it helps to bring in their own words from the German Relation of the Leipzig Colloquy.

There the Brandenburg and Hessian theologians voluntarily confessed with mouth and heart the 1530 Confession delivered to Charles V at Augsburg, and said they would subscribe it — even the Saxon Elector’s exemplar in the Augapfel — whenever and wherever asked, because they and their lords already bound themselves to it in church and school.
227: (2.) At the colloquy’s end both sides signal why they met: to see how far they agree in the Augsburg Confession’s articles, and what hope remains of a closer union later — to enlarge Christ’s true church and quench the papists’ confidence drawn from Protestant division — while stipulating Christian love to one another in the meantime.

Their Relation words put it thus: the colloquy was meant first to learn, in summary, whether and how far both parties are one in the twenty-eight Augsburg articles, and whether further conferences of peace-loving theologians, with Christian high authority, might raise a nearer holding-together; and both sides’ theologians would show each other Christian love going forward, faithfully and without deceit.
228: (3.) Finally, in the third year afterward the Imperial Estates gathered at Frankfurt am Main not only approved the Leipzig Colloquy, but — judging they would not be cheated of the Leipzig theologians’ hope — sanctioned by a special decree that Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked in the Estates’ public name to keep the Protestant peace business begun at Leipzig going through more moderate theologians’ work, and to bring it to a happy end.
Because few know that decree, we set it out here in the words printed in John Dury’s Prodromus Irenicorum, p. 1.
229: Decree of the Evangelical Estates made at Frankfurt.

John Dury again laid before the Evangelical Estates’ convention (Circles present, and absent princes’ legates) the business of union and fraternal reconciliation among Evangelicals inside and outside the Empire on the fundamental heads of Christian evangelical religion — a matter floated before — and in a notable deputies’ sitting he was heard by all confederated Estates, citing many leading theologians and academies of either party in Germany, France, England, and Transylvania on how that Christian unity-aim might be reached.

The six Circles unanimously judged the work grateful to the God of peace, praiseworthy, most necessary, and useful to evangelical churches — yet also a heavy business for which many deputies present had no instructions. So the present legates and deputies undertook to report home faithfully the proposal and the theologians’ opinions shared with them.
230: Some legates also offered friendly proposals: that the Circles forward at once a declaration on Dury’s proposed procedure and on a peaceable theologians’ colloquy — modeled on the Leipzig collation three years earlier among Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian-Cassel electoral theologians — and that the Electors invite foreign princes and kings by letters.

Others usefully proposed that, saving each Elector’s, prince’s, and Estate’s rights, Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked to continue that Leipzig-friendly collation and call a convention where other peaceable theologians of either party can sit or send judgments — aiming at a modest Christian consensus-confession on every salvation-foundation head, while parking scholastic fights on the rest.

Several also agreed that meanwhile both sides should use Christian moderation and mildness in teaching and writing, and that public prayers for the work be framed in both parties’ churches, committing the business to God Most High.
This recess was made in witness of that. Done at Frankfurt am Main, 14 September 1634.
